newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS-Czech cbank begins easing, crown holds steady.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Czech cbank begins easing, crown holds steady.

text.p: The Czech central bank on Monday took its first step toward easing its grip on the embattled crown, but analysts said the move had little effect on the currency with the market now focused on the country's turbulent political scene.
The Czech National Bank (CNB) dropped its repo rate to 45 percent from a previous 75 percent in two separate operations early on Monday.
The crown, under heavy selling pressure over the last two weeks, eased some 50 basis points after the rate cut, though it regained all of its losses as a lack of liquidity kept speculators at bay.

But analysts said the economic and monetary factors that have pushed the crown to record lows in recent weeks have been overshadowed by a recent wave of political turmoil that has forced major cabinet changes and opposition calls for a vote of no-confidence against the government.
"The Czech economy is facing a very tough lesson and any sign, even a small one, of political instability makes the whole situation worse," said Petr Benes of Nomura International.
The crown firmed against the mark to stand at 19.131 to the mark and 32.944 to the dollar at 1300 GMT, slightly stronger than morning levels.

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, in a dramatic acknowledgement of the Czech economy's problems, announced last Wednesday sweeping cabinet changes -- including the sacking of his Finance Minister -- and a six-point recovery plan, including more spending cuts and a public sector wage freeze.
The moves followed two turbulent weeks for the currency as investors, alarmed at yawning trade and current account deficits as well as political uncertainty, dumped the crown.

The government package is intended to restore balance to the economy and stabilise the currency. The cuts will need the approval of parliament where the ruling three-party coalition has the slenderest majority.

Opposition leader Milos Zeman has often called for Klaus's resignation, and last week said he would table a no-confidence vote against the government in July, while the premier himself said on Saturday that he may call his own confidence vote as early as next week.
Analysts said that the central bank still needed to make several more moves on interest rates and that this might prompt investors to go on the offensive and once again push the crown lower.
"Now we've moved into expectations of what's going to happen with the government and expectations of a rate cut. It means a weaker crown," said Petr Kukla of Girocredit Bank.

Two weeks ago, the central bank moved to shore up the crown by raising its Lombard rate to 50 percent from 14 percent, and its repo rate to 75 percent from 12.9 percent, while cutting off non-residents's access to crowns.

On Monday, continued selling pressure on the crown forced the CNB to abolish the bands within which the crown moves against a basket of marks and dollars (65 pct marks/35 pct dollars), calling the new system a "controlled float".
It also raised its discount rate to 13 percent from 10.5. The currency immediately weakened some eight percent before recouping some of the losses in an illiquid market.
"At the end of the day, the most important thing for the crown is political stability" said one Frankfurt-based dealer.
"The market still has its eyes on rates, but it is waiting on this. Politics are much less controllable, and the market knows this and fears it more," he added.
